text:
The 95% upper credible limit on the detectable Pop III caustic transit rate is $\lambda_{95} = 0.87\ {\rm cluster}^{-1}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ [S1][S3].

**How it was derived**
- The authors searched three JWST/NIRCam epochs of MACS0416 for caustic transits at $7\leq z\leq17$ and found no new Pop III candidates [S1].
- They modelled the transit rate as a Poisson process with a conjugate Gamma prior, $\lambda\sim{\rm Gamma}(1, 3.125\,{\rm yr})$. That prior has a mean of 0.32 yr⁻¹, which is the reference rate from Windhorst et al. (2018) (W18) [S3].
- With zero events in an effective observing time of about 0.34 yr, the posterior is ${\rm Gamma}(1, 3.465)$ [S3].
- The posterior mean is 0.29 cluster⁻¹ yr⁻¹, or about one expected transit per 3.5 cluster-years of monitoring. The 95% upper limit, defined by $P(\lambda<\lambda_{95}\mid{\rm data})=0.95$, is 0.87 [S3].

**Caveats**
The limit is tied to the W18 $100\,M_\odot$ reference case. It only covers transits bright enough to be seen at a single-epoch JWST depth of about AB ≃ 28.5 mag [S3].

**What follows from it**
Using the W18 scaling, the null result means the observer-frame 2 μm Pop III sky surface brightness must be fainter than $32.8\pm0.61$ mag arcsec⁻². If a cluster transverse velocity of 2000 km s⁻¹ is assumed, this becomes ≥ $33.6\pm0.6$ mag arcsec⁻², which implies a Pop III surface density of ≲ 600 stars arcsec⁻² [S2].

S3.where: Constraints on the 2 Sky-SB and Caustic Transits of Pop III stars > Interpreting the Pop III Non-Detection

S4.where: Constraints on the 2 Sky-SB and Caustic Transits of Pop III stars > Constraints on the 2 Pop III star sky-SB

**37 cases.** The authors checked the DESI host redshifts against the spectroscopic redshifts reported on TNS for the identified supernovae, and only 37 disagreed [S2].

**Why:** most of the mismatches came from host confusion. A background or foreground galaxy sitting at a small angular separation from the true host was picked by mistake [S2].

**Context:**
- The check used the retrospective 2020–2024 sample. About 17,600 events were visually confirmed on Legacy Surveys cutouts, and about 16,800 remained after duplicates and mis-identified sources were removed [S2].
- The generous 30 search radius used for this sample probably increased the chance of nearby-galaxy confusion. At $z\approx0.05$ that radius roughly matches a 30 kpc disc [S2]. (The radius unit was lost in extraction; it is presumably arcseconds.)
- The pipeline's host rule is built to avoid this exact problem. In the example the paper shows, the nearest spectrum belongs to a small background galaxy, and the rule instead assigns the larger foreground spiral whose light contains the transient [S5]. On its calibration set, the rule picks the wrong host 0.4% of the time [S1].

The sources don't say how big the subset of supernovae with TNS redshifts was, so I can't give an exact discrepancy rate. They also don't explain the minority of mismatches that weren't host confusion.

General-relativistic calculations find a seed black hole of only about $\mathcal{O}(10^{-8})$ of the halo mass, measured at the point where an apparent horizon forms [S1].

**How the GR result was obtained.** Gu+ 2026 added general-relativistic effects directly to the late-time core-collapse evolution [S1]. They extended the earlier quasi-equilibrium treatment by putting an SIDM heat-flux term into the energy-momentum tensor, using the Misner-Sharp formalism, and evolving the system out of equilibrium [S1]. A strong outward heat flux drives a lot of mass out during the final plunge, which is why the seed ends up so small [S1].

**Agreement with another approach.** Gad-Nasr+ 2024 got a similar answer without GR. They used scaling relations between late core-collapse phases and the deep short-mean-free-path stage, evaluated where the core speed reaches about $c/3$ (the onset of relativistic instability) [S1]. They found seeds of $\mathcal{O}(10^{-9})$–$\mathcal{O}(10^{-8})$ of the halo mass, i.e. stellar-mass seed black holes, depending on the cross-section model [S1]. The paper says the two methods independently agree on an initial seed of about $\mathcal{O}(10^{-8})\,M_{\rm halo}$ [S2].

**Seed mass vs. final mass.** This tiny figure is only the initial seed that the relativistic instability produces directly. It is not the mass after growth. Earlier estimates of the mass reached by the end of rapid core collapse were about $\mathcal{O}(10^{-2})\,M_{\rm halo}$ [S2]. The paper's own N-body accretion model finds a converged dark-matter-accreted mass of about 5%–12% of the halo mass [S6].

S1.where: Mass growth of SIDM seeded black hole > Comparison with other works

**About \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-8})\) of the halo mass** — i.e., a stellar-mass seed.

Gu+ 2026 (labeled `gu26`) incorporated general-relativistic effects directly into the late-time core-collapse evolution, adding an SIDM heat-flux term to the energy–momentum tensor via the Misner–Sharp formalism, and evolved the system until an apparent horizon formed. Their result: an apparent-horizon BH seed mass of merely \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-8})\) of the halo mass [S1]. The introduction states that this GR approach and the independent scaling framework of Gad-Nasr+ 2024 (which finds \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-9})\)–\(\mathcal{O}(10^{-8})\) depending on cross-section model) agree on an initial seed of \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-8})\) of the halo mass [S1, S2]. This is consistent with the schematic in [F2], where "Gu+ 2026 (GR horizon seed)" sits at \(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\rm halo}\sim10^{-8}\), near the \(10^{-8}\) gridline.

Note the contrast with the later, macroscopic growth: the SMFP/gravothermal-core estimates of Feng+ 2021 are \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-2})\) [S2, F2], and this work's converged long-term DM-accreted mass is \(\sim5\%\!-\!12\%\,M_{\rm halo}\) [S6].

Overall, the best-fit dark QCD (DQCD) model sits closer to the DESI DR2 BAO points than Planck-only ΛCDM, and does slightly better than ΛCDM fit jointly to Planck and DESI [F2]. The plot shows each distance as a percentage shift relative to the ΛCDM prediction from Planck alone, so ΛCDM fit to Planck only is the zero line [F2].

**Compared with Planck-only ΛCDM (the zero line):** Most DESI DR2 points fall below zero, by about 1–4% at low redshift. The DQCD curves are also below zero at low z. As z increases they move back towards zero, so they track the data much better than the zero line does. The authors say these parameters "significantly reduce the tension with DESI measurements relative to the Planck-only ΛCDM cosmology" [S2].

**Panel by panel (values read from the image):**
- **$D_M/r_d$:** DQCD starts near −2.4% at low z and rises to about −0.8% at z ≈ 2.5. That is below the Planck+DESI ΛCDM curve, which goes from about −1.6% to −0.6%. The lower DQCD curve fits the points near −2% at z ≈ 0.7–1.3 better. It misses the high points at z ≈ 0.5 (+0.6%) and z ≈ 1.5 (+0.7%) [F2].
- **$D_V/r_d$:** DQCD runs from about −2.3% to −0.4%. It is a little below the ΛCDM curve at low z, and the two curves meet above z ≈ 2. Neither curve reaches the low point at z ≈ 0.7 (about −2.6%) [F2].
- **$D_H/r_d$:** DQCD starts near −2.2% and crosses zero around z ≈ 1.3. It ends slightly positive at high z (about +0.5%), a bit above ΛCDM (about +0.2%). Both curves fall short of the very low points at z ≈ 0.5–0.7 (about −3.5% to −4%) [F2].

**Compared with ΛCDM fit to Planck+DESI:** The two sets of curves are similar. DQCD differs mainly in having a steeper drop at low z. The paper describes DQCD as "mildly outperform[ing]" ΛCDM here [S2]. The figure shows the curves, not a χ² or any other number for that comparison.

The figure caption also notes that the three distance ratios are not independent measurements, so the three panels should not be read as three separate tests [F2].

S1.where: Appendix: Details on the cosmological inference setup

text:
**Short answer:** In [F2], the DQCD best fit (dashed) predicts distance ratios that sit **below** the Planck+DESI ΛCDM best fit (dotted) at low redshift — i.e. a larger suppression of $D_M/r_d$, $D_V/r_d$, and $D_H/r_d$ relative to the Planck-only ΛCDM baseline (zero of the y-axis) — which moves the prediction toward the DESI DR2 data points, which are themselves mostly negative at $z\lesssim1.5$. At high $z$ the two curves converge and both approach zero.

**Detail from the figure:**
- $D_M/r_d$ (left panel, blue): DQCD goes from $\sim-2.3\%$ at $z\simeq0.5$ to $\sim-0.7\%$ at $z\simeq2.3$; the ΛCDM Planck+DESI fit instead runs from $\sim-1.6\%$ to $\sim-0.6\%$, so DQCD lies closer to the DESI points at $z\approx0.7$–$1.5$ (which are near $-2\%$).
- $D_V/r_d$ (middle, green): same pattern — DQCD $\sim-2.3\%$ at $z\simeq0.5$ vs ΛCDM $\sim-1.6\%$, converging to $\sim-0.4\%$ by $z\simeq2.3$; again DQCD tracks the low-$z$ DESI points better.
- $D_H/r_d$ (right, red): both models are negative at low $z$ and turn slightly positive at high $z$; DQCD is the more negative of the two below $z\sim1$, though the two lowest-$z$ DESI points ($\approx-4\%$ with large errors) are below even the DQCD curve.
- Neither model reproduces the individual scatter of the DESI points (e.g. the near-zero/high points at $z\simeq1.3$–$1.5$), and the caption notes the three DESI measurements are not independent.

This matches the text's claim that DQCD "significantly reduce[s] the tension with DESI measurements relative to the Planck-only ΛCDM cosmology, and mildly outperform[s] ΛCDM with parameters fit to both Planck and DESI" [S2].

S1.where: Appendix: Details on the cosmological inference setup

Reading [F1], the medians run from about 70.8 to 73.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. All of them fall between the Planck and SH0ES bands or inside the SH0ES band, and none is close to Planck.

**Range across the reconstruction × selection grid** (linear warp, volume prior; approximate values read from the plot) [F1]:
- **No peculiar-velocity model:** about 72.7–72.9 for distance selection and about 73.1–73.5 for redshift selection. These are the highest values.
- **Linear (Carrick+2015) reconstruction:** about 71.5–71.6 for distance selection and about 72.2–72.3 for redshift selection.
- **Non-linear (Manticore-Local) reconstruction:** about 70.8 for distance selection and about 71.5–71.6 for redshift selection. The text gives these exactly as $70.8^{+3.6}_{-3.4}$ / $71.6^{+3.8}_{-3.5}$ on one baseline table and $70.8^{+3.7}_{-3.5}$ / $71.5^{+3.9}_{-3.5}$ on the other [S2].

The two baseline spot tables (circles and squares) give nearly the same values. Redshift selection is always about 0.7–0.8 higher than distance selection [S2]. Adding a reconstruction lowers $H_0$, and the non-linear field lowers it most [S4].

**Position relative to the bands:**
- The runs without a reconstruction have medians inside the SH0ES band (about 72.3–74) [F1].
- The runs with a reconstruction sit between the two bands, closer to SH0ES. Each error bar (about ±3.5) covers the SH0ES band, and the lower ends reach about 67–68, near the edge of the Planck band at about 67.4 [F1].
- The paper's fiducial result (redshift selection, Manticore reconstruction, about 71.5–71.6 ± 3.6) is 1.1σ above the CMB value and 0.4σ below SH0ES [S1].
- Every variant is below the earlier MCP value of about 73.9 (Pesce+2020) shown in the same figure [F1].

**The high-threshold signal is strongly modulated in all the simulated halos, and it peaks around late May to early June, slightly before the LZ event date of June 16.**

**Size of the modulation**
- The plotted quantity is $M(t)=g_{\rm high}(t)/\max(g_{\rm high})$, where $g_{\rm high}$ is the mean inverse speed integrated over $v_{\min}>700$ km/s [S1, F1]. Every curve therefore tops out at 1.0.
- Reading the figure, the SHM curve falls from 1.0 at its peak to about 0.39 around early December. That means the winter rate is roughly 40% of the summer rate [F1].
- The 68% band of the TNG-50 halos follows the SHM closely. Its winter minimum spans roughly 0.2–0.55 [F1]. The paper says that on average the halos have "an almost identical modulation to the fiducial SHM" [S2].
- The 95% and 100% bands reach all the way down to 0 for parts of the year [F1]. Some halos switch on much more sharply with the season, because they slightly prefer suppressed high-speed tails [S2]. In about 5% of halos the rate "can almost vanish for three-quarters of the year," even at this fairly modest threshold [S2]. In the figure, the lowest envelope is non-zero only from about March to August [F1].
- This matches the paper's statement that above about 700 km/s the modulation amplitude can approach 100% [S1].

**When it peaks**
- The "Peak day" histogram is concentrated from about mid-May to early June, with its highest bin near the end of May or start of June. That is just before the LZ event marker at June 16 [F1, S4].
- A few outliers peak in April, late June, or January [F1]. The text describes this as most halos peaking "around June, but with a spread of about a month" [S2].
- The SHM curve also peaks around early June [F1].

The numbers above are my approximate readings from the image, not values stated in the text.

The figure implies a boson mass of about $m_\psi \simeq 2.2\times10^{-22}$ eV ($m_{22}\simeq 2.2$) for galaxy formation starting at $z_f = 15.1$. This value comes from the calibrated red curve, which is pinned to the first galaxy appearing at z = 13 in the Schive+14 $\psi$DM simulation (red star) [F1]. The abstract gives the same value with uncertainties: $m_\psi = 2.2_{-0.3}^{+0.4}\times10^{-22}$ eV, tied to a Jeans mass of $\sim4\times10^9 M_\odot$ being overcome at z = 15 [S4].

Other curves on the same plot:
- **Uncalibrated Jeans relation (blue dashed):** This curve is where $M_{min}$ equals $M_{exp}$ [S5]. Reading the plot, it crosses z ≈ 15.1 a bit higher, at roughly $m_{22}\approx 2.6$–2.7 [F1]. That number is my estimate from the image, not one the paper states.
- **Alternative method that integrates the halo mass function (green curve):** The caption gives a lower value, $m_{22}\simeq 1.7$, for $z_f = 15.1$ [F1].
- **Independent constraints (horizontal dotted lines):** These cover roughly $m_{22}\approx 1.8$–2.9. They come from dwarf spheroidal cores, transients in the Dragon Arc lensed galaxy, and a diffusion-based estimate [F1]. They agree with the ~2.2 value, which the paper notes is consistent with lensing and dynamical estimates [S2][S3].

**m₂₂ ≈ 2.2, i.e. m_ψ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻²² eV** (with the calibrated relation), for z_f = 15.1.

Details from [F1]:

- The red **calibrated z_onset–m₂₂ relation** crosses z_f ≈ 15 at m₂₂ ≈ 2.2; the caption states this explicitly: "implying mass of m₂₂ ≃ 2.2 for z_f = 15.1 after calibration (red curve)" [F1].
- The green solid curve, the alternative **HMF-based locus**, also agrees with the simulation but instead gives m₂₂ ≃ 1.7 at z_f = 15.1 [F1]. In the figure, the green dashed curve sits slightly below the red one at z ≈ 15.
- Both values are consistent with the independent lensing/dynamics estimates shown as horizontal dashed lines in the 1.5–3 range [F1], and with the abstract value m_ψ = 2.2₋₀.₃⁺⁰·⁴ × 10⁻²² eV at z = 15 [S4].
- The red star marks the Schive+14 simulation halo at z = 13, which the scaling reproduces [F1].

The two quantities respond to mass very differently. The fitted UV slope barely changes across the broad-line mass range, while $R_{\rm sph}/R_{1400}$ falls steadily, roughly as the inverse of mass [F1].

**(a) Fitted slope $\beta_{\rm UV}$**
- At low mass the slope is shallow. It rises past −2.0 below about $5\times10^5\,M_\odot$, because the higher supply rate pushes $R_{\rm sph}$ into the region that emits the UV [S6].
- As mass increases the slope steepens and then levels off near −2.28 above about $3\times10^6\,M_\odot$, where the transition sits well inside the emitting region [S6]. It stays slightly shallower than the standard-disk value of −7/3 [F1].
- At the central N iv] benchmark mass (about $1.6\times10^6\,M_\odot$), my reading of the plot gives $\beta_{\rm UV}\approx-2.22$, inside the observed $-2.26\pm0.10$ band [S3], [F1].
- Across most of the 0.3 dex benchmark range, the slope changes by less than the measurement error [S6]. The only real constraint is at the low-mass end: the model drops out of the $1\sigma$ interval below $M_{\beta_{\rm UV}}=(0.94$–$1.21)\times10^6\,M_\odot$. If the colour correction varies, that bound widens to $(0.60$–$1.60)\times10^6\,M_\odot$ [S6]. So the slope alone only requires $M_{\rm BH}\gtrsim10^6\,M_\odot$ [S2].

**(b) Radius ratio $R_{\rm sph}/R_{1400}$**
- Above roughly $8\times10^5\,M_\odot$, the ratio falls monotonically. From the plot it is about 0.5 at the benchmark mass and about 0.1 near $8\times10^6\,M_\odot$ [F1]. The paper's analytic estimate at the benchmark mass is 0.47–0.60 [S4].
- Where the two radii stay distinct, the composite-model envelope follows the analytic criterion (red dashed line). The envelope sits slightly above that line for most of the range [S2], [F1].
- Near the separation mass $M_{\rm sep}$ (about $7\times10^5\,M_\odot$), the curve flattens at 1. The paper explains this as the numerical emission peak locking onto the flux break at $R_{\rm sph}$ [S2]. In the plot this plateau runs from about $5.5\times10^5$ to $8\times10^5\,M_\odot$. Below that the envelope rises above 1 again, which the text doesn't mention [F1].

The paper's conclusion is that $\beta_{\rm UV}$, the usual basis for the Eddington mass $M_{\rm E}$, carries little information about mass, while the radius ratio responds strongly even though it isn't measured directly. Pinning down the inner accretion state therefore needs a handle on $R_{\rm sph}$, not a more precise $\beta_{\rm UV}$ [S2].

S2.where: Results > What the ultraviolet slope does constrain

S3.where: Results > The ultraviolet slope cannot distinguish the inner states

text:
As \(M_{\rm BH}\) increases, both quantities decrease, but in different ways [F1]:

- **Fitted UV slope \(\beta_{\rm UV}\)** (left panel): it steepens from roughly \(-2.0\) at the lowest plotted masses toward \(\sim -2.28\), then flattens/saturates above \(\sim 3\times10^{6}\,M_\odot\). The standard thin-disk value \(-7/3\) is shown as a gray dashed line, and the observed \(1\sigma\) band is broad, so the slope changes little across most of the benchmark mass range [F1a][S6].
- **Radius ratio \(R_{\rm sph}/R_{1400}\)** (right panel): it declines monotonically, approximately inversely with mass. It is \(>1\) at low mass, crosses unity at the separation mass \(M_{\rm sep}\) (red dotted vertical line), and falls well below unity at high mass. The composite model tracks the analytic criterion where the two radii are distinct and saturates near unity around \(M_{\rm sep}\) [F1b][S2].

So increasing \(M_{\rm BH}\) moves the spherization radius inward relative to the UV-emitting region, while \(\beta_{\rm UV}\) changes only modestly and saturates—making the radial ratio a cleaner mass diagnostic than the slope [F1][S2].

S2.where: Results > What the ultraviolet slope does constrain

In the $g_{BL}$–$m_{Z'}$ figure, the allowed (blue) region is bounded by four constraints [F1]:

- **Left and upper-left: the current LHC limit.** The solid red curve is the upper bound on $g_{BL}$ from the ATLAS Run-2 $Z'$ dilepton resonance search [F1], [S4].
- **Bottom: the lower LZ cross-section contour.** The lower green line marks $\sigma_{\rm SI}=10^{-46}$ cm². The LZ event is reproduced between this line and the $\sigma_{\rm SI}=10^{-45}$ cm² line [S1], [F1].
- **Top: perturbativity, plus a short stretch of the upper LZ contour.** The black dashed curve at $g_{BL}\approx0.45$ comes from requiring no Landau pole below $M_{\rm Pl}$, $g_{BL}(m_{Z'}) < \sqrt{8\pi^2/[11\ln(M_{\rm Pl}/m_{Z'})]}$ [S5]. From the plot, the upper green ($10^{-45}$ cm²) line appears to form the top edge only near $m_{Z'}\approx5.5$ TeV, just before it crosses the perturbativity line [F1].
- **Right: the projected HL-LHC reach.** The red dashed curve is the Run-2 limit scaled by $\sqrt{137/3000}$ [S5], and the paper states that it closes the region on the right [S4].

The relic-density requirement (solid black curve) is a lower bound on $g_{BL}$ that the whole blue region satisfies [S4], [F3]. It is not a visible edge, though: near the blue region it sits at only about $g_{BL}\sim0.04$–0.05, well below the region [F1].

Reading the plot, the blue region spans roughly $m_{Z'}\approx5$–7 TeV and $g_{BL}\approx0.2$–0.45 [F1].

In [F1] (the $g_{BL}$–$m_{Z^\prime}$ plane of the $Z^\prime_{B-L}$ endothermic Majorana DM scenario) the allowed region is the **blue shaded band**, and it is bounded by four different constraints:

- **Lower/left boundary — relic density + LZ event:** the solid black curve is the minimum $g_{BL}$ needed to reproduce $\Omega_{\rm DM}h^2\simeq0.12$ for each $m_{Z^\prime}$, and the two solid green lines are the spin-independent cross sections $\sigma_{\rm SI}=10^{-45}\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ (upper) and $10^{-46}\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ (lower) relevant to the LZ event; the band between them is where the LZ interaction strength can be realized [F1][S1][S4]. The relic requirement sets a lower bound because below it even the resonant ($m_{\rm DM}\simeq m_{Z^\prime}/2$) enhancement cannot deplete the abundance enough [S3][S4][F3].
- **Left boundary — current LHC:** the solid red curve is the upper bound on $g_{BL}$ from the ATLAS Run-2 $Z^\prime\to\ell^+\ell^-$ dilepton resonance search; the allowed region must lie to its right (larger $m_{Z^\prime}$ for fixed $g_{BL}$) [F1][S4].
- **Right boundary — future LHC:** the dashed red curve is the projected HL-LHC reach, scaling as $\mathcal{L}^{-1/2}$ ($137\to3000\ \mathrm{fb}^{-1}$), i.e. $g_{BL}^{\rm HL\text{-}LHC}\simeq g_{BL}^{\rm Run\text{-}2}\sqrt{137/3000}$; beyond it the parameter point would be excluded [S5][F1][S4].
- **Upper boundary — perturbativity:** the black dashed curve is the Landau-pole bound $g_{BL}<\sqrt{8\pi^2/[11\ln(M_{\rm Pl}/m_{Z^\prime})]}$, which in the figure is an essentially flat line at $g_{BL}\approx0.45$ [S5][F1].

Reading numbers off [F1], the blue region spans roughly $m_{Z^\prime}\approx 4.3$–$7.2$ TeV with $g_{BL}\approx0.2$–$0.5$, sitting between the relic-density/LZ contours from below and the perturbativity and HL-LHC limits from above/right [F1][S4].

The papers mostly agree that the event needs dark matter whose spectrum peaks at high recoil energy without a pile-up of low-energy events, and **endothermic inelastic dark matter** is the leading answer. They differ in how that is achieved and in what the DM must be.

**The problem they all address.** LZ saw one nuclear-recoil candidate at $E_R = 248 \pm 23_{\rm stat} \pm 23_{\rm sys}$ keV in 2.84 ton·yr, in a region with almost no expected background [S1, S2]. It disfavours background-only at a global $2.6\sigma$ [S5, S6]. Ordinary elastic scattering would give a spectrum that falls steeply with energy. So the difficulty is not the high energy itself but the absence of accompanying low-energy events [S1, S5]. Even elastic scattering would need $q \simeq 246$ MeV, meaning $m_\chi \gtrsim 79$ GeV [S5].

**1. Endothermic inelastic DM (the dominant reading).** The DM upscatters to a heavier state, $\chi_1 + N \to \chi_2 + N$ with $\delta = m_{\chi_2} - m_{\chi_1} > 0$. This makes low-energy recoils kinematically impossible [S1]. Exothermic down-scattering ($\delta < 0$) can also explain the event [S1]. The requirements are:
- WIMP-like masses above about 200 GeV with $\delta \sim \mathcal{O}(100)$ keV [S5, S6].
- **Higgsino version:** about 1.1 TeV, where Higgsinos are thermal relics with the right abundance. They have two neutral Majorana states split by less than 1 MeV and scatter through $Z$ exchange [S2, S4]. A benchmark with $m_\chi = 1$ TeV and $\delta = 375$ keV fits the event [S3, S4]. However, it is in tension with IceCube limits on DM captured in the Sun [S4, S6]. It may also conflict with LZ itself, because it predicts many events in LZ's empty ~350–680 keV sideband [S4]. That sideband is uncalibrated for nuclear recoils, which makes this hard to settle [S4].
- **Radiative Dirac-neutrino-mass model (arXiv:2609.15027):** a singlet–doublet mixing parameter $\kappa$ generates the neutrino mass and also controls the inelastic rate [F3]. The viable region is $m_{\chi_1} \approx 400$ GeV–1.2 TeV with $\delta_{RI} \simeq 340$–360 keV. There it reproduces the relic abundance, neutrino masses of the right order, and about one signal event [F3]. Its spectra rise to a peak near 248 keV and then fall smoothly [F3]. In the plotted ~500 GeV benchmarks, the peak sits slightly below 248 keV, around 215–220 keV.

**2. Boosted DM (arXiv:2609.14799).** Light, relativistic DM supplies the momentum instead of a heavy mass. This only works if the interaction depends on momentum [S5]:
- With the scalar–scalar and pseudoscalar–scalar operators, 99% and 92% of events fall below 150 keV, which conflicts with the empty low-energy region [S5].
- With the pseudoscalar–pseudoscalar operator, 75% of events fall above 150 keV [S5], and the spectrum has a pronounced high-energy tail [F2].

The same paper finds that inelastic spectra put only 6–17% of events below 150 keV for every operator, and that the preferred $\delta$ shrinks going from $\mathcal{O}_{ss}$ to $\mathcal{O}_{ps}$ to $\mathcal{O}_{pp}$ [S5]. A handful more events should distinguish the two scenarios with the full LZ exposure [S5].

**3. Astrophysical caveat (arXiv:2609.21444).** Because inelastic scattering depends on the fastest DM particles, the result is sensitive to the high-velocity tail of the Milky Way halo [S3]. Using velocity distributions from simulated halos (TNG-50) instead of the Standard Halo Model reshapes the 1 TeV / 375 keV spectrum considerably [F1]. Averaged over halos, more weight moves below the observed energy and less goes into the high-energy sideband [S4]. That would ease the sideband tension but not resolve it [S4]. In the figure, the event's energy sits in a dip between a low-energy and a high-energy peak [F1].

**4. Modified gravity and non-DM ideas.** One paper is titled "Did LZ see modified gravity?" [S6], but the excerpt only covers the Higgsino and other DM interpretations and their problems [S6]. It doesn't say what the modified-gravity proposal is or what it requires. Other papers propose alternative and non-DM explanations [S2, S6], but the sources only cite them without giving any details.

S1.where: The LZ event and inelastic dark matter

The responses cluster around **inelastic (endothermic) DM**, with **boosted DM**, **Higgsino-like DM**, a **radiative neutrino-mass model**, and **non-DM/modified-gravity** alternatives. The LZ input is a single candidate at \(E_R=248\pm23_{\rm stat}\pm23_{\rm sys}\,\mathrm{keV}\) in \(2.84\,\mathrm{ton\,yr}\), with no low-energy excess and \(2.6\sigma\) global significance against background-only [S1,S5,S6].

- **Endothermic inelastic DM** — the most common interpretation. DM up-scatters, \(\chi_1+N\to\chi_2+N\), with \(\delta=m_{\chi_2}-m_{\chi_1}>0\); low-energy recoils are kinematically forbidden, so a single high-energy recoil is natural [S1]. It requires a mass splitting and relies on the high-velocity tail of the Galactic DM distribution; the 2609.21444 paper uses \(m_\chi=1\,\mathrm{TeV}\), \(\delta=375\,\mathrm{keV}\) as an example and notes that halo-to-halo velocity variations can substantially distort the spectrum [S3,S4,F1]. That example is Higgsino-like: a \(\sim1.1\,\mathrm{TeV}\) thermal relic with two neutral Majorana states split by a sub-MeV mass and \(Z\)-mediated inelastic scattering [S2]. However, this parameter choice is in tension with IceCube and potentially with LZ’s empty \(350\)–\(680\,\mathrm{keV}\) sideband [S4]. The 2609.14799 paper finds inelastic spectra near 248 keV for all effective operators, with only \(6\)–\(17\%\) of events below 150 keV, and a preferred \(\delta\sim\mathcal{O}(100)\,\mathrm{keV}\) that decreases from \(\mathcal{O}_{ss}\) to \(\mathcal{O}_{ps}\) to \(\mathcal{O}_{pp}\) [S5]. The 2609.15118 paper likewise notes that inelastic WIMP DM above \(\mathcal{O}(200\,\mathrm{GeV})\) can accommodate the event [S6].

- **Boosted DM** — the alternative emphasized by 2609.14799. A light relativistic DM flux supplies the required momentum transfer \(q\simeq246\,\mathrm{MeV}\) without producing the missing low-energy recoil excess [S5]. It requires a light relativistic DM component and is strongly operator-dependent: for \(\mathcal{O}_{ss}\) and \(\mathcal{O}_{ps}\), \(99\%\) and \(92\%\) of events lie below 150 keV, whereas for \(\mathcal{O}_{pp}\), \(75\%\) lie above it [S5]. Figure [F2] shows the boosted spectra (solid) having much larger low-energy components and stronger operator dependence than the inelastic spectra (dashed), which are concentrated near the LZ energy [F2].

- **Inelastic DM tied to radiative Dirac neutrino masses** — the 2609.15027 paper interprets the event as endothermic inelastic DM in a model where the singlet–doublet mixing \(\kappa\) generates the Dirac neutrino mass and controls the inelastic rate, while the splitting \(\delta_{RI}\) fixes the recoil-spectrum position [F3]. It requires \(m_{\chi_1}\sim400\,\mathrm{GeV}\)–\(1.2\,\mathrm{TeV}\) and \(\delta_{RI}\simeq340\)–\(360\,\mathrm{keV}\), while reproducing the relic abundance, light neutrino masses, and \(N_{\rm SR}\simeq1\) in the LZ exposure; the spectra peak near 248 keV and fall beyond it [F3].

- **Modified gravity / non-DM alternatives** — 2609.15118 is framed as “Did LZ see modified gravity?” and lists non-DM possibilities, but the supplied text does not specify the modified-gravity mechanism or its requirements; it mainly notes that the minimal Higgsino interpretation faces challenges from solar-capture constraints [S6].

Elastic halo DM is not treated as a viable explanation: it would give a monotonically falling spectrum with an accompanying low-energy excess, and the required momentum transfer only implies \(m_\chi\gtrsim79\,\mathrm{GeV}\) [S5].

The two papers take complementary approaches. The HETDEX paper (arXiv:2609.16134) works spectroscopically at z~2: it looks for strong He II λ1640 with no UV metal lines and reports actual candidates. The LATED paper (arXiv:2609.24588) is a photometric framework at z≲7: it uses rest-frame optical lines in Lyα-selected samples. In the provided excerpts it is checked against known candidates but does not report a new candidate sample.

## 1. HETDEX: He II λ1640 with no UV metal lines (arXiv:2609.16134)

**Strategy.** The search is for Lyα emitters showing strong nebular He II λ1640 while C IV, N V and O III] are weak or absent [S2].
- He II λ1640 needs photons above 54.4 eV, which normal metal-enriched populations produce few of. That makes it the most direct rest-frame UV probe of a hard ionizing spectrum [S1].
- Missing metal lines point to very low abundance [S2].
- The point is to test for hard radiation and weak enrichment at the same time [S1].

**Findings.**
- The candidates have a number density of about 30 Gpc⁻³ [S5].
- The authors assume about 6×10⁵ M⊙ of Pop III stars per candidate and a He II visibility time of about 3 Myr. That gives a rough star-formation rate density (SFRD) of about 6×10⁻⁹ M⊙ yr⁻¹ Mpc⁻³ [S5].
- This is below earlier He II-selected limits at z~2–4: Nagao 2008 gives ≲5×10⁻⁶ and Cassata 2013 about 10⁻⁶. It is far below JWST estimates at z~6–7, and below theoretical predictions of 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁶ for late Pop III formation [S5].
- The authors say this is a candidate SFRD for a rare, deliberately restrictive phase, not a completeness-corrected census [S5].
- Their interpretation: the spectra fit stellar photoionization in extremely metal-poor gas, with a Pop III-like spectrum as the most extreme case [S2]. A fully pristine population at z~2 would be surprising, but is plausible if metal mixing is patchy [S2].

## 2. LATED: photometric selection from Lyα-emitter samples (arXiv:2609.24588)

**Strategy.** The search targets "belated" pristine pockets at z≲7 down to z≈2, rather than z>10 [F2]. It starts from existing tomographic Lyα-emitter catalogues and applies four stages [F2]:
1. Redshift windows where the filters cover [O III]+Hβ, Hα and continuum bands.
2. An EW(Hα)–O/H colour diagram.
3. Vetoes for contaminants, including a flag for little red dots (LRDs).
4. Line-flux and line-ratio inference from photometry, released as the Python package `lated`.

**Model basis.** Pop III templates sit in an extreme corner of the diagram, with EW(Hα) ≈ 2700–4150 Å and [O III]5007/Hβ ≲ 0.02 at Z=0 [S6]. Switching to a second Pop III model family moves the selection envelope by ≲0.04 mag, so the selection is insensitive to the model choice [S6].

**Completeness.** With 5σ depths of 28 mag, recovery is about 100% brighter than 25 mag. Half of targets are recovered at 27.93 mag in Hα, which is the only real gate; the continuum and [O III]+Hβ curves are just shifted by typical Pop III colours [F3].

**Checks against known candidates.** The excerpts show the method applied to three published objects:

| Candidate | z | Photometric [O III]/Hβ (2σ) | Spectroscopic value |
|---|---|---|---|
| CR3 | 3.19 | <0.78 | <0.89 |
| AMORE6 | 5.73 | <2.52 (weak, low continuum S/N); the authors' own deblended photometry is much tighter | <0.33 |
| GLIMPSE-16043 | — | <2.08 (median 0.88) | 1.78±0.18 |

For CR3 the photometric limit is tighter than the spectroscopic one [F1].

## Shared caveat

The LATED paper argues that neither method can prove an object is Pop III [S3]. Observations only set upper limits on metallicity, and these stay above the theoretical critical value Z_crit ≲ 10⁻³·⁵ Z⊙ [S3]. Also, He II with no metal lines can come from other sources: very massive low-metallicity stars, stripped binaries, X-ray binaries, or shocks [S3]. A stronger Pop III claim would need 12+log(O/H) ≲ 7, no sign of an active nucleus, and [O III]/Hβ < 0.1, ideally with He II detected. Even then the object is still only a candidate [S3].

S3.where: Future prospects > From candidates to confirmation

S5.where: Physical Interpretation > Comparison to Previous Observational & Theoretical Constraints

**Two different strategies:**

1. **Direct UV emission-line spectroscopy of Lyα emitters (HETDEX, arXiv:2609.16134).**  
   This search targets **nebular He II λ1640**, which requires ionizing photons above 54.4 eV, together with **absent UV metal lines** in HETDEX Lyα emitters at \(z\sim2\) [S1]. The logic is to require both hard ionizing radiation and very weak metal enrichment simultaneously [S1][S2].  
   **What it found:** a candidate population of He II-bright, metal-line-poor systems with a rough number density of \(\sim30\ \mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}\) [S5]. For an assumed Pop III mass of \(\sim6\times10^5\,M_\odot\) per candidate and a \(\sim3\) Myr burst, this implies a Pop III stellar mass density \(\sim0.018\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}\) and a candidate SFRD \(\sim6\times10^{-9}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}\) [S5]. That is below earlier He II limits/estimates and far below JWST-based estimates at \(z\sim6\)–7, and below some theoretical late Pop III expectations [S5]. The authors stress this is an observed candidate SFRD for a restrictive search, not a completeness-corrected census [S5].

2. **Lyα-anchored photometric preselection plus line-ratio inference (LATED, arXiv:2609.24588).**  
   This is a **tomographic Lyα-emitter selection** followed by photometric identification of extremely metal-poor/metal-free candidates [F2]. The parent Lyα emitters are already biased toward low stellar mass, low metallicity, low dust, and young starbursts [F2]. LATED then applies four stages: redshift windows with filters covering \([O III]+H\beta\), Hα, and continuum; an **EW(Hα)–O/H diagram** using \(m_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}-m_{\mathrm{cont}}\) versus \(m_{\mathrm{[OIII]}}-m_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}\); multi-wavelength contaminant vetoes; and photometric emission-line flux/ratio inference [F2]. The output is a ranked Pop III candidate sample for spectroscopic follow-up [F2].  
   **What it found so far:** the provided sources describe the framework and worked examples rather than a new confirmed sample. For the published metal-free candidate **CR3** at \(z=3.19\), the three-band photometric inference gives \([O III]/H\beta<0.78\) at \(2\sigma\), tighter than the spectroscopic bound \(<0.89\) [F1]. For **AMORE6** at \(z=5.73\), it gives a weak \(<2.52\) at \(2\sigma\), consistent with the metal-poor classification [F1]. For **GLIMPSE-16043**, it returns \([O III]/H\beta<2.08\) at \(2\sigma\), consistent with the later spectroscopic value \(1.78\pm0.18\) [F1]. Recovery tests show the color stage is complete at the bright end and has a half-recovery point at \(m=27.93\) in the Hα band for a \(5\sigma\) depth of 28 mag [F3].

**Shared caveat:** neither approach proves a truly metal-free population. Observations constrain metallicity only from above, and even nebular He II with undetected metal lines can be produced by very massive low-metallicity stars, stripped binaries, X-ray binaries, or shocks [S3]. A stronger Pop III designation would require \([O III]/H\beta<0.1\), ideally with nebular He II, but even that remains a candidate rather than proof [S3].

S3.where: Future prospects > From candidates to confirmation

S5.where: Physical Interpretation > Comparison to Previous Observational & Theoretical Constraints

In both papers the injected energy heats the gas, but it is detected in different ways. In the dwarf-galaxy paper, it shows up as missing low-ionization absorption lines in quasar spectra that pass through the galaxy's outer gas. In the 21-cm paper, it shows up as a weaker and patchier 21-cm absorption signal at high redshift.

**1. Dwarf-galaxy circumgalactic medium (arXiv:2609.15748)**
- **Model:** Heating is set by an effective rate $Γ_{\rm heat}$, with $\dot u_{\rm heat} = \rho_{\rm DM} c^2 Γ_{\rm heat}$. It is applied in RAMSES simulations of an isolated dwarf galaxy similar to WLM [S1][S5].
- **Effect on the gas:** The diffuse gas around the galaxy becomes hotter and more spread out. The dense disk gas and the star formation rate stay nearly unchanged [S1][F1].
  - In the temperature–density plot [F2], the lowest-density gas sits at about $10^4$–$10^5$ K with no dark matter heating.
  - At $\log Γ_{\rm heat} = -25$ that gas rises to roughly $10^6$ K or more. The gas at $\rho \gtrsim 10^{-25}$ g cm$^{-3}$ looks much the same in every run.
- **Observable:** Quasar sightlines through the galaxy's halo, observed with far-ultraviolet spectroscopy, would show lower absorption column densities [S1][S3]. For $Γ_{\rm heat} = 10^{-27}$–$10^{-25}$ s$^{-1}$, compared with the run without heating [S1]:

| Species | Suppression of column density |
|---|---|
| Neutral hydrogen at 10 kpc | 0.6 to 3.9 dex |
| C II, Si II | 4.1 and 5.5 dex |
| C IV, Si IV | 2.2 and 3.0 dex |

- **Scope:** The simulations use a decay-like source. Annihilation heating scales as $\rho_{\rm DM}^2$ and is more concentrated toward the centre, so applying these limits to annihilation models would need a dedicated simulation [S4].

**2. 21-cm signal with annihilation in host halos and subhalos (arXiv:2609.21479)**
- **Effect on the gas:** Energy from annihilation raises the gas temperature, which makes the 21-cm absorption trough shallower [F3].
- **What the figure shows:** [F3] covers annihilation to $e^+e^-$ with $m_\chi = 10^9$ eV and $\langle σv\rangle = 10^{-27}$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$.
  - Without dark matter, the absorption trough sits at about $z \sim 13$–20, reaching roughly −60 mK.
  - With annihilation in host halos only, the change $\Delta T_{21}$ is positive, up to about +50 mK, over that same redshift range. In other words, the absorption becomes weaker.
- **Spatial pattern:** The change is not a uniform shift. It follows how many halos there are locally, so it alters the 21-cm fluctuations. That is why the paper connects it to forecasts for 21-cm power-spectrum measurements [F3].
- **Channel dependence:** The $e^+e^-$ channel gives a larger change than the photon channel [F3].
- **Gap in the sources:** I only have this one figure from that paper. The sources don't give the numbers for the case that includes subhalos, the photon-channel results, or the actual power-spectrum sensitivity forecasts.

S4.where: Discussion and Conclusions > Mapping the Heating Rate to Particle Models

S5.where: Discussion and Conclusions > Mapping the Heating Rate to Particle Models

text:
**Two different observables, both driven by raising the gas temperature.**

**Paper 1 (dwarf-galaxy CGM as a calorimeter; arXiv:2609.15748):** The signal is a *deficit* in absorption-line columns seen against background quasars. For Γ_heat = 10⁻²⁷–10⁻²⁵ s⁻¹, the neutral-hydrogen column at 10 kpc is suppressed by 0.6 to 3.9 dex relative to the control run, C II and Si II columns drop by 4.1 and 5.5 dex, and C IV and Si IV by 2.2 and 3.0 dex [S1]. These are accessible to FUV spectroscopy of quasar sightlines through dwarf halos, since FUV metal resonance lines trace gas temperature and ionization state [S3]. The suppression is confined to the diffuse CGM: the simulations show a hotter, more diffuse CGM with the dense disk and SFR nearly unchanged [S1, F1], and in phase space it is the low-density gas that shifts to higher temperature while the high-density ISM stays put [F2]. The temperature maps make this visible directly — the outer CGM goes from ~10⁴ K in the control to ~10⁶–10⁷ K at log(Γ_heat/s⁻¹) = −25, while the HI density in the halo fades accordingly [F1].

**Paper 2 (21-cm constraints on S-wave annihilation; arXiv:2609.21479, [F3]):** Here the signature is in the 21-cm brightness temperature: energy deposition from annihilation raises the gas temperature and **reduces the depth of the 21-cm absorption signal** [F3]. The effect is spatially dependent rather than a uniform shift, because the annihilation source follows the local halo abundance — which also means it modifies 21-cm fluctuations and hence power-spectrum observables [F3]. The residual lightcone ("host only − baseline") is positive, up to roughly +50 mK, over z ≈ 12–20, i.e. the absorption trough is filled in [F3]. The e⁺e⁻ channel produces a larger residual amplitude than the photon channel [F3].

So: in the dwarf-CGM case, look for *weaker metal and HI absorption lines* toward background quasars [S1, S3]; in the 21-cm case, look for a *shallower, spatially patchy 21-cm absorption trough* at high redshift [F3].

S4.where: Discussion and Conclusions > Mapping the Heating Rate to Particle Models

The sources don't include a dark QCD paper. Every passage and figure provided comes from one paper, arXiv:2609.17684 (the megamaser reanalysis), so I can't say what H₀ a dark QCD paper reports, how it was obtained, or how its uncertainty compares. Here is the megamaser side only.

**How the megamaser value is obtained**
- The five discs of the Megamaser Cosmology Project (MCP) are each fitted with a warped Keplerian disc model to get a distance. The five distances are then combined into a constraint on H₀ [S1, S2].
- The paper uses a uniform-in-volume distance prior together with a matching treatment of the selection function. Because the sample's true selection is unknown, it tests two simple selection models: one based on distance and one on redshift [S1].
- The fiducial setup uses a redshift selection threshold, a peculiar-velocity reconstruction and a linear warp [S1].
- As a check, the pipeline reproduces the Pesce et al. (2020) distances to within 0.3σ when given the same inputs [S1].

**Result and uncertainties**
- H₀ = 71.5 and 71.6 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ on the two baseline spot tables, each ±3.6 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ statistical [S1].
- That is 1.1σ above the CMB value and 0.4σ below the SH0ES distance-ladder value [S1].
- Modelling choices matter at a similar level. Across eleven variants (selection threshold, peculiar-velocity reconstruction, distance prior), H₀ shifts by 2.4–2.7 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ within either baseline table [S5].
- The original catalogues give 69.3^{+3.7}_{-3.6} km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, about 2.3 lower. Of that offset, 1.8–2.1 comes from updated measurements, mainly in NGC 6264 and NGC 6323, and the rest from removing spots [S5]. The authors say this shows the effect of the MCP reanalysis and should not be read as an alternative analysis or an extra systematic uncertainty [S5].

If you can share the dark QCD paper's text, I can make the comparison.

S6.where: Results > Distance sensitivity to the spot measurements and clipping

**No dark QCD paper is among the provided sources**, so I cannot state its \(H_0\) value, how it is obtained, or compare its uncertainty to the megamaser result. The sources here contain only the megamaser reanalysis (arXiv:2609.17684). What that paper reports:

**Value and method.** From the five megamaser discs of the Megamaser Cosmology Project, the reanalysis obtains \(H_0 = 71.5\) and \(71.6~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}\) on its two baseline spot tables, with \(\pm 3.6~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}\) statistical uncertainty [S1]. These come from a forward model of warped Keplerian disc physics fitted to spot catalogues, combined with a uniform-in-volume distance prior, a self-consistent selection-function treatment, and peculiar-velocity modelling; the fiducial configuration uses a redshift selection threshold, a reconstruction, and a linear warp [S1]. The disc modelling reproduces the Pesce et al. (2020) distances to within \(0.3\sigma\) when given their inputs [S1].

**Consistency and variants.** The baseline values sit \(1.1\sigma\) above the CMB value and \(0.4\sigma\) below SH0ES [S1]. Using the catalogue tables instead gives \(69.3^{+3.7}_{-3.6}~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}\), about \(2.3~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}\) lower, driven mainly by updated measurements for NGC 6264 and NGC 6323 plus spot removal [S5]. Across eleven modelling variants (selection threshold, peculiar-velocity reconstruction, distance prior) the spread within a baseline table is only \(2.4\)–\(2.7~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}\) [S5], i.e., well below the \(\pm3.6\) statistical error. [F2] shows these values over the reconstruction × selection grid for the P20 and Revised-clipped tables, alongside the Planck and SH0ES reference bands.

The Euclid paper doesn't derive any constraint on primordial black hole abundance. The excerpts from it [S3, S6] never mention PBHs or $f_{\rm PBH}$.

What the Euclid paper covers is a blind challenge comparing nine algorithms that detect galaxy clusters through weak lensing, tested on 1200 deg² of Euclid-like simulated data from DEMNUni-Cov [S3, S6]. It picked four methods (AMICO-WL, DoG, O21, W234). On their own these reach about 10% completeness at 90% mean purity. Combined, they do about twice as well, passing 70% completeness for low-redshift, high-mass clusters. The paper expects about 2500 weak-lensing-detected clusters in Euclid DR1 [S6].

The PBH constraints in the sources come from two other papers:
- **SMILE VLBI milli-lensing paper (arXiv:2609.20329):** if no events are detected, it projects a 95% upper limit of $f_{\rm PBH} \lesssim 0.12\%$ near $M_{\rm PBH} \sim \mathcal{O}(10^7)\,M_\odot$, across the $10^6$–$10^9\,M_\odot$ range. That is about an order of magnitude tighter than earlier VLBI limits. A single confirmed event would loosen it to 0.20% [S1, S2].
- **LUX-ZEPLIN paper (arXiv:2609.29462):** it sets 90% C.L. limits on PBHs that evaporate, for masses of $2\times10^{11}$–$2\times10^{13}$ g. The limit reaches $f_{\rm PBH} \lesssim 10^{-6}$ near $2\times10^{11}$ g [F2].

The Euclid paper derives no constraint on primordial black hole abundance. It is a methods paper on detecting galaxy clusters through weak lensing, not a PBH study: nine detection algorithms were tested in a blind challenge on 1200 deg² of Euclid-like DEMNUni-Cov simulations, with the pre-selected four methods (AMICO-WL, DoG, O21, W234) reaching ~10% completeness at 90% mean purity individually and >70% completeness for low-redshift, high-mass clusters when combined, extrapolating to ~2500 clusters in Euclid DR1 [S6]. Its introduction frames the motivation only in terms of characterizing the cluster population with WL-selected samples [S3].

The PBH abundance constraints in the provided sources come instead from the SMILE VLBI milli-lensing paper — e.g. a projected 95% upper limit $f_{\rm PBH}\lesssim 0.12\%$ for $10^6$–$10^9\,M_\odot$ under optimistic zero-detection conditions [S1], with the strongest limit near $M_{\rm PBH}\sim\mathcal{O}(10^7)\,M_\odot$ [S2] — and from the separate LUX-ZEPLIN paper, which constrains much lighter PBHs ($M_{\rm PBH}\sim2\times10^{11}$–$2\times10^{13}$ g) down to $f_{\rm PBH}\lesssim10^{-6}$ [F2].

The sources give no dark-photon kinetic-mixing bound. The passages from this paper (arXiv:2609.15967) never mention dark photons, kinetic mixing or any particle-physics constraint.

The paper is about accretion physics. Its main results are:

- **A criterion for where the inner flow changes.** It derives the closed-form ratio $R_{\rm sph}/R_{\nu}=0.385\,(\nu L_\nu^{\rm iso}/L_{\rm Edd})/\cos i$, which compares the radius where the flow becomes supercritical with the radius that produces the observed ultraviolet light [S3].
- **The transition sits inside the ultraviolet-emitting region.** At the N iv]-based mass of $10^{6.2}\,M_\odot$, $R_{\rm sph}/R_{1400}=0.47$–$0.60$ [S3, S6]. Matching the observed continuum then requires $\dot M_{\rm out}=3.1$–$4.4\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ [S2, S5].
- **The ultraviolet slope barely changes.** Replacing the inner $\sim10^{3}r_{\rm g}$ with a supercritical flow shifts $\beta_{\rm UV}$ by only $+0.08$ to $+0.11$ [S3].
- **The mass bound is weak.** On its own, the slope only implies $M_{\rm BH}\gtrsim10^{6}\,M_\odot$. That is an order of magnitude below the continuum Eddington mass of $1.12\times10^{7}\,M_\odot$ [S3, F1].

If you want a dark-photon kinetic-mixing bound, it would have to come from a different paper, which isn't among these sources.

S2.where: Results > The low-mass branch is necessarily supercritical

S6.where: Results > The transition lies inside the ultraviolet-emitting region
